subcategory: Diesel Fuel System / Fuel Pressure Regulator
title: Fuel Pressure Regulator 1 Control Circuit Malfunction
shortDescription: The ECM detected a general electrical fault in the fuel pressure regulator 1 control circuit.
fullDescription:
P0090 indicates an electrical malfunction in the circuit that controls the high-pressure fuel pump's pressure regulator solenoid (also called FCA, SCV, or MPROP on diesel engines). The ECM monitors current and voltage on the control wire; when readings fall outside expected ranges, this code sets.

On common-rail diesels this solenoid meters the amount of fuel entering the high-pressure pump, directly controlling rail pressure. A failure can cause no-start, stalling, or limp mode. The fault is usually electrical (wiring, connector, solenoid coil) rather than mechanical.
safetyImpact: Engine may enter limp mode, lose power on highway, or fail to start. Avoid hard acceleration.

causes.cause: Damaged wiring or connector at the regulator

fixSteps.title: Scan and freeze-frame
fixSteps.instruction: Read code and freeze-frame data with a bidirectional scanner.

fixSteps.title: Inspect connector
fixSteps.instruction: Unplug the regulator connector and check for corrosion, bent pins, oil contamination.

fixSteps.title: Measure coil resistance
fixSteps.instruction: Check solenoid resistance against spec (typically 2-6 ohms).

fixSteps.title: Replace regulator
fixSteps.instruction: Replace fuel pressure regulator / SCV if out of spec.

faq.q: Can I drive with P0090?
faq.a: Short trips at low load may be possible but limp mode and stalling are common; repair promptly.

subcategory: Diesel Fuel System / Fuel Pressure Regulator
title: Fuel Pressure Regulator 1 Control Circuit Low
shortDescription: Voltage on the fuel pressure regulator 1 control circuit is below the expected threshold.
fullDescription:
P0091 sets when the ECM detects that the control line voltage for the fuel pressure regulator is too low, suggesting a short to ground or an open in the coil. On diesel common-rail engines this typically causes uncontrolled rail pressure and limp mode.

Common culprits are a chafed wire shorting against the engine block, a failed solenoid with an internal short, or a ground leak in the harness near the high-pressure pump.
safetyImpact: Possible stalling, no-start, or sudden power loss. Drive cautiously and repair promptly.

causes.cause: Short to ground in control wire

fixSteps.title: Check wiring
fixSteps.instruction: Inspect harness for chafing or contact with hot surfaces.

fixSteps.title: Test for short to ground
fixSteps.instruction: With connector unplugged, test control wire to ground for continuity.

fixSteps.title: Replace solenoid
fixSteps.instruction: Replace fuel pressure regulator if coil is shorted.

faq.q: Is this a wiring issue or sensor issue?
faq.a: Test wiring first — shorts to ground are the most common cause of the 'Low' variant.

subcategory: Diesel Fuel System / Fuel Pressure Regulator
title: Fuel Pressure Regulator 1 Control Circuit High
shortDescription: Voltage on the fuel pressure regulator 1 control circuit is above the expected threshold.
fullDescription:
P0092 indicates the ECM sees an abnormally high voltage on the regulator control circuit. This is typically caused by an open circuit, a short to battery voltage, or a disconnected solenoid.

On diesels this prevents the ECM from commanding the pump, leading to excessive or insufficient rail pressure depending on the regulator's default position.
safetyImpact: Engine may stall or enter limp mode without warning.

fixSteps.title: Verify connector seated
fixSteps.instruction: Make sure the regulator plug is fully latched.

fixSteps.title: Continuity test
fixSteps.instruction: Test control wire from ECM to regulator for continuity.

fixSteps.title: Replace regulator
fixSteps.instruction: Replace solenoid if coil is open.

faq.q: Could a blown fuse cause P0092?
faq.a: Yes — check any fuses powering the high-pressure pump circuit before replacing parts.

title: Fuel System Leak Detected - Large Leak
shortDescription: The ECM detected a large fuel system leak, often a rail or return-line failure.
fullDescription:
P0093 is set when the ECM sees rail pressure drop faster than expected or fuel consumption inconsistent with commanded injector pulse width. On diesel common-rail systems it typically indicates a cracked high-pressure line, a leaking injector return, or a failed rail pressure relief valve.

The engine may start then stall as pressure bleeds off, or refuse to start altogether.
safetyImpact: Fuel leaks are a fire hazard and can cause engine damage. Stop driving if fuel smell present.

fixSteps.title: Visual inspection
fixSteps.instruction: Look for wet spots on rail, lines, and injector tops.

fixSteps.title: Return flow test
fixSteps.instruction: Measure injector return volume to identify a leaking injector.

fixSteps.title: Replace leaking component
fixSteps.instruction: Replace the failed line, injector, or relief valve.

faq.q: Can I find the leak myself?
faq.a: External leaks often, but internal injector leaks need a return-flow test.

title: Fuel System Leak Detected - Small Leak
shortDescription: The ECM detected a small fuel system leak.
fullDescription:
P0094 indicates a minor leak in the high-pressure fuel system — typically a slightly weeping injector seal, hairline crack in a line, or worn O-ring. Rail pressure may still be maintained but the ECM sees abnormal decay rates during shutdown or idle.

Small leaks can grow quickly on diesels due to extremely high rail pressures (25,000+ psi). Address promptly.
safetyImpact: Fuel leaks are a fire risk even when small.

fixSteps.title: UV dye test
fixSteps.instruction: Add diesel-safe UV dye and look for leak paths.

fixSteps.title: Re-torque fittings
fixSteps.instruction: Check and re-torque line fittings to spec.

fixSteps.title: Replace seals
fixSteps.instruction: Replace the offending injector seal or O-ring.

faq.q: Will it pass emissions with P0094?
faq.a: Usually not — the code must be cleared and not returned before a drive cycle completes.

title: Intake Air Temperature Sensor 2 Circuit Malfunction
shortDescription: General fault in the second intake air temperature sensor circuit.
fullDescription:
P0095 indicates the ECM detected a problem with the IAT sensor 2 circuit. On turbocharged and diesel engines, IAT2 is often placed after the intercooler to measure charge air temperature — critical for boost and injection timing control.

Faults are typically caused by a failed sensor, damaged wiring near hot intake piping, or a disconnected plug after intercooler service.
safetyImpact: Boost or fuel trim may be limited, reducing power.

fixSteps.title: Inspect sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Locate IAT2 (usually on charge pipe after intercooler) and inspect wiring.

fixSteps.title: Check signal
fixSteps.instruction: Use scan tool live data to compare IAT1 vs IAT2 during cold start.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Replace IAT2 if out of spec.

faq.q: Is IAT2 the same as MAF?
faq.a: No — MAF measures airflow mass; IAT2 is a temperature-only sensor, usually a thermistor.

title: SCR NOx Catalyst Efficiency Below Threshold Bank 1
shortDescription: The SCR catalyst is not reducing NOx emissions effectively enough to pass OBD monitoring.
fullDescription:
P20EE sets when the downstream NOx sensor reading is too close to the upstream sensor reading, indicating the SCR (Selective Catalytic Reduction) catalyst is not converting NOx effectively. This is a federal emissions code on modern diesels (post-2010).

Common causes include SCR catalyst contamination or aging, DEF (diesel exhaust fluid) quality issues, failed NOx sensors giving false data, or insufficient DEF dosing. Left unfixed, most diesels will progressively derate and eventually enter a 5 mph limp mode.
safetyImpact: Engine will derate and eventually limit speed to 5 mph in most diesels.

causes.cause: DEF dosing pump or injector problem

fixSteps.title: Verify DEF quality
fixSteps.instruction: Test DEF concentration with a refractometer (should be 32.5%).

fixSteps.title: Check NOx sensors
fixSteps.instruction: Compare upstream and downstream NOx readings at steady cruise.

fixSteps.title: Inspect dosing system
fixSteps.instruction: Verify DEF injector spray pattern and pump pressure.

fixSteps.title: Replace SCR catalyst
fixSteps.instruction: If catalyst is contaminated, replace assembly.

faq.q: Can I delete the SCR to avoid this code?
faq.a: No — SCR deletes are illegal in the US and carry heavy fines. Fix the root cause.

title: Reductant Quality Performance
shortDescription: The ECM detected that DEF (diesel exhaust fluid) quality is below specification.
fullDescription:
P207F is set when the ECM's reductant quality monitor determines that DEF is not performing as expected. This can be from contaminated DEF, wrong fluid (water or diesel in the DEF tank), or degraded DEF that has been stored too long or frozen.

The quality check uses NOx sensor feedback during dosing events to infer DEF concentration. Failures lead to progressive power derates.
safetyImpact: Derate with eventual 5 mph limp mode on most diesels.

fixSteps.title: Drain and refill DEF
fixSteps.instruction: Empty the DEF tank completely and refill with fresh, in-date DEF.

fixSteps.title: Test DEF concentration
fixSteps.instruction: Use a refractometer to confirm 32.5% urea.

fixSteps.title: Replace quality sensor
fixSteps.instruction: If fluid is good, replace DEF quality sensor.

faq.q: Can I use distilled water if I'm out of DEF?
faq.a: No — DEF is a precise 32.5% urea solution; water will trigger quality codes and can damage the SCR.

title: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance Bank 1 Sensor 1
shortDescription: The EGT sensor reading is outside the expected range or response time.
fullDescription:
P2080 indicates the exhaust gas temperature sensor upstream of the DPF or SCR is reading out of expected range, or responding too slowly to temperature changes. EGT sensors are critical for controlling regeneration of the DPF and for protecting aftertreatment components from overheating.

Failures can be caused by a slow-responding or drifted sensor, soot contamination, or wiring degradation from heat cycling.
safetyImpact: Regen events may be blocked, leading to progressive DPF soot buildup.

fixSteps.title: Compare sensors
fixSteps.instruction: Compare EGT1 vs EGT2 / EGT3 at steady load to spot drift.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Replace EGT1 with OE-quality part.

faq.q: Will this block regen?
faq.a: Often yes — the ECM requires valid EGT data to command an active regen.

title: A Camshaft Position Actuator Control Circuit Low Bank 1
shortDescription: Voltage on the bank 1 intake camshaft actuator circuit is below threshold.
fullDescription:
P2088 sets when the ECM detects low voltage (usually a short to ground or an open) on the bank 1 intake camshaft position actuator solenoid. Variable valve timing solenoids control oil flow to the cam phaser; when the control circuit fails the cam cannot be adjusted dynamically.

Symptoms include rough idle, reduced power, and knock or ping under load.
safetyImpact: Possible rough running and reduced performance; no immediate safety risk.

causes.cause: Short to ground in control wire

fixSteps.title: Check oil condition
fixSteps.instruction: Confirm oil is fresh and at correct level.

fixSteps.title: Test solenoid
fixSteps.instruction: Measure coil resistance; compare to spec.

fixSteps.title: Replace solenoid
fixSteps.instruction: Replace VVT solenoid if faulty.

faq.q: Can I delay repair?
faq.a: Short-term yes, but prolonged VVT malfunction can cause timing chain stress on some engines.

title: Post Catalyst Fuel Trim System Too Lean Bank 1
shortDescription: The post-catalyst oxygen sensor detects a lean condition that fuel trims cannot correct.
fullDescription:
P2096 indicates the downstream O2 sensor is reporting a persistently lean exhaust after the catalytic converter on bank 1. The ECM has attempted to correct fuel trim but cannot bring the readings into range.

Common causes include exhaust leaks upstream of the rear O2, a failed downstream sensor, or a catalyst that is leaking air. On turbo applications, a leaking wastegate or cracked downpipe can mimic this fault.
safetyImpact: Increased emissions; possible mild drivability issues.

causes.cause: Exhaust leak before/at rear O2 sensor
Weak fuel pump or dirty injector

fixSteps.title: Smoke test exhaust
fixSteps.instruction: Pressurize exhaust and look for leaks around flex pipe and flange.

fixSteps.title: Check live O2 data
fixSteps.instruction: Watch downstream O2 voltage at steady cruise.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Replace downstream O2 if it's the fault.

faq.q: Can a bad catalyst cause P2096?
faq.a: Yes — a cracked cat or leak at the downpipe introduces oxygen downstream.

title: Post Catalyst Fuel Trim System Too Rich Bank 1
shortDescription: The post-catalyst oxygen sensor detects a rich condition fuel trims cannot correct.
fullDescription:
P2097 is the counterpart of P2096 and sets when the rear O2 sensor reports a persistently rich mixture. Because the rear sensor mostly monitors catalyst efficiency, a 'rich' reading often indicates a failed sensor, a contaminated catalyst, or overly rich fuel control from upstream issues.

On turbo vehicles, fuel in the oil crankcase dilution or a leaking injector can enrich the rear sensor signal.
safetyImpact: Emissions exceedance; potential long-term catalyst damage.

fixSteps.title: Check fuel pressure
fixSteps.instruction: Verify fuel pressure against spec.

fixSteps.title: Inspect injectors
fixSteps.instruction: Check for leaking or stuck-open injectors.

fixSteps.title: Replace rear O2
fixSteps.instruction: Swap downstream sensor if diagnostics point there.

faq.q: Could fuel in the oil cause this?
faq.a: Yes — crankcase fuel dilution vented through PCV can enrich the downstream reading.

title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control A Performance - Mechanical
shortDescription: Mechanical issue with the variable-geometry turbo (VGT) vane actuator.
fullDescription:
P226F indicates the ECM commanded a VGT vane position but mechanical feedback indicates the vanes did not move as expected. This is extremely common on diesel trucks where soot fouls the VGT vane mechanism, causing them to stick.

The condition is often recoverable with solvent cleaning or a VGT clean procedure, but severe fouling may require turbo removal and inspection.
safetyImpact: Boost control lost; engine derate and reduced towing capacity.

fixSteps.title: Scan and actuate
fixSteps.instruction: Use bidirectional scan tool to cycle VGT and watch actual vs commanded position.

fixSteps.title: Clean VGT
fixSteps.instruction: Perform VGT cleaning with manufacturer-approved solvent.

fixSteps.title: Replace turbo
fixSteps.instruction: If cleaning fails, replace turbo or actuator.

faq.q: Can regens prevent this?
faq.a: Yes — driving long enough to complete regens reduces soot and VGT sticking.

title: Air Leak Between Throttle Body and Intake Valves
shortDescription: The ECM detected unmetered air entering the intake downstream of the throttle.
fullDescription:
P2282 sets when the ECM concludes there is an air leak between the throttle and intake valves based on MAF/MAP disagreement and fuel trim behavior. On turbocharged engines, this often means a cracked charge pipe, blown intercooler hose, or torn intake boot.

Smoke-testing the intake is the fastest diagnostic.
safetyImpact: Reduced boost and power; potential long-term damage if ingesting debris.

fixSteps.title: Smoke test
fixSteps.instruction: Pressurize intake and look for smoke escape points.

fixSteps.title: Tighten / replace clamps
fixSteps.instruction: Re-clamp or replace damaged hoses.

fixSteps.title: Replace intercooler
fixSteps.instruction: If intercooler is leaking, replace assembly.

faq.q: Why is smoke testing so useful?
faq.a: Boost leaks often open only under pressure — a smoke test replicates that without the engine running.

title: Diesel Particulate Filter Differential Pressure Too Low
shortDescription: Pressure difference across the DPF is lower than expected.
fullDescription:
P244A sets when the delta-P sensor reports less pressure drop across the DPF than the ECM expects. Common causes include a broken/melted DPF substrate, a disconnected delta-P hose, or a failed pressure sensor.

A low reading can mask a failing DPF, so the ECM flags it to protect downstream components.
safetyImpact: Emissions non-compliance; potential derate.

fixSteps.title: Inspect hoses
fixSteps.instruction: Check delta-P hose routing and condition.

fixSteps.title: Test sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Verify delta-P sensor readings at known engine states.

fixSteps.title: Inspect DPF
fixSteps.instruction: Borescope DPF inlet for substrate damage.

faq.q: Will a DPF clean fix this?
faq.a: Only if the substrate is intact — broken DPFs must be replaced.

title: Diesel Particulate Filter Differential Pressure Too High
shortDescription: Pressure difference across the DPF exceeds the expected threshold.
fullDescription:
P244B indicates excessive backpressure across the DPF, typically from soot or ash loading that regeneration cannot clear. The ECM commands a forced regen or derates the engine when the condition persists.

Frequent short-trip driving prevents passive regen from completing and accelerates soot accumulation. Ash buildup (from lubricant additives) is permanent and eventually requires DPF cleaning or replacement.
safetyImpact: Power derating; possible limp mode if ignored.

fixSteps.title: Force regen
fixSteps.instruction: Perform a stationary forced regen using scan tool.

fixSteps.title: Highway drive cycle
fixSteps.instruction: Sustained highway driving to complete passive regen.

fixSteps.title: DPF cleaning service
fixSteps.instruction: Professional off-vehicle DPF cleaning (pneumatic or thermal).

fixSteps.title: Replace DPF
fixSteps.instruction: Replace if cleaning cannot restore backpressure.

faq.q: How often does a DPF need cleaning?
faq.a: Typically every 150,000-250,000 miles depending on duty cycle.

title: Diesel Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor A Circuit
shortDescription: General fault in the DPF pressure sensor A circuit.
fullDescription:
P2452 sets when the ECM detects an electrical fault in the DPF (delta-P) pressure sensor A circuit. The sensor measures the pressure drop across the DPF to estimate soot load.

Faults are commonly caused by clogged pressure reference tubes, failed sensor, or wiring damaged by exhaust heat.
safetyImpact: DPF monitoring lost; regen logic impaired.

fixSteps.title: Inspect tubes
fixSteps.instruction: Remove and check pressure reference tubes for soot clog.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Replace delta-P sensor if faulty.

faq.q: Can I clean tubes myself?
faq.a: Yes — use compressed air to clear soot, but replace if they are cracked.

title: Diesel Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
shortDescription: DPF pressure sensor A reading is outside expected range.
fullDescription:
P2453 sets when the delta-P sensor reading disagrees with expected values based on engine state. For example, reading significant pressure at idle with a clean filter indicates drift, while near-zero pressure under load suggests a restriction issue.

Check the pressure tubes before replacing the sensor.
safetyImpact: Regen cycles may be mistimed.

fixSteps.title: Compare to spec
fixSteps.instruction: Observe delta-P reading at cold idle; should be near zero.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Replace if drifted.

faq.q: Can extreme cold cause false trips?
faq.a: Yes — very cold temps can cause temporary sensor offset; clear and retest after warmup.

title: Diesel Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor A Circuit Low
shortDescription: DPF pressure sensor A signal is below the expected low threshold.
fullDescription: P2454 indicates the delta-P sensor voltage is lower than allowed. This usually means a short to ground, an open in the 5V reference, or a failed sensor stuck at minimum reading.
safetyImpact: DPF monitoring impaired.

fixSteps.title: Check reference voltage
fixSteps.instruction: Probe 5V reference at sensor connector.

fixSteps.title: Check signal
fixSteps.instruction: Verify signal wire continuity and absence of shorts.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Replace delta-P sensor.

faq.q: What voltage should the signal show?
faq.a: Typically 0.5-4.5V range; at idle expect around 0.5-1V.

title: Diesel Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor A Circuit High
shortDescription: DPF pressure sensor A signal is above the expected high threshold.
fullDescription:
P2455 sets when the delta-P signal voltage is too high, indicating a short to voltage, open ground on the sensor, or a sensor failed at its maximum output.

Check wiring and ground first — sensor failures are common but cheaper to rule out after the circuit is confirmed good.
safetyImpact: DPF monitoring impaired.

fixSteps.title: Check ground
fixSteps.instruction: Verify sensor ground continuity to chassis.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Replace delta-P sensor if circuit is good.

faq.q: Can corrosion trigger this?
faq.a: Yes — corroded ground pin is a frequent cause of 'circuit high' codes.

title: Diesel Particulate Filter Restriction - Soot Accumulation
shortDescription: DPF is restricted by soot beyond the regeneration recovery threshold.
fullDescription:
P2463 indicates the DPF is carrying a soot load that cannot be reduced by normal active regeneration. This is most often caused by repeated aborted regens (short trips, idle time), a failed fuel dosing system, or mechanical issues preventing EGT from reaching regen temps.

Most vehicles will require a forced/service regen or manual DPF cleaning to recover.
safetyImpact: Power derate; potential limp mode.

causes.cause: Low EGT (failed glow plug / injector / EGR stuck open)

fixSteps.title: Highway drive
fixSteps.instruction: Sustained 55+ mph for 30+ minutes to trigger regen.

fixSteps.title: Force regen
fixSteps.instruction: Use scan tool to command stationary regen.

fixSteps.title: DPF cleaning
fixSteps.instruction: Professional DPF cleaning if regen won't complete.

faq.q: Can I use DPF additives?
faq.a: Some help with passive regen but cannot fix heavy soot loading on their own.

title: Diesel Particulate Filter Differential Pressure Too Low Bank 2
shortDescription: Delta pressure across DPF on bank 2 is lower than expected.
fullDescription: P2464 is the bank 2 version of P244A — applicable to dual-bank diesel applications (rare in light duty, common on large displacement applications). A broken substrate or disconnected pressure line are the usual causes.
safetyImpact: Emissions non-compliance on bank 2 aftertreatment.

fixSteps.title: Inspect tubes
fixSteps.instruction: Verify pressure tube connections at bank 2.

fixSteps.title: Borescope DPF
fixSteps.instruction: Check DPF integrity.

faq.q: Does this apply to V-configuration diesels?
faq.a: Yes — bank 2 codes appear on vehicles with dual DPFs.

title: Diesel Particulate Filter Differential Pressure Too High Bank 2
shortDescription: Delta pressure across DPF on bank 2 is higher than expected.
fullDescription: P2465 is the bank 2 version of P244B. The bank 2 DPF is soot-loaded beyond recovery. Apply the same diagnostic and repair logic: force regen, then clean or replace.
safetyImpact: Bank 2 derate; potential limp mode.

fixSteps.title: Force regen
fixSteps.instruction: Command stationary regen with scan tool.

fixSteps.title: DPF cleaning
fixSteps.instruction: Off-vehicle cleaning if regen fails.

faq.q: Can I run just on bank 1?
faq.a: No — both aftertreatment systems must function for emissions compliance.

title: Diesel Particulate Filter Restriction - Exhaust Pressure Too High
shortDescription: Exhaust backpressure exceeded safe limits during regeneration.
fullDescription:
P246C sets when the ECM detects exhaust overpressure during or after a regen attempt. This can damage turbos and rupture gaskets, so the ECM derates aggressively.

Root causes include a physically restricted DPF (often from oil contamination), collapsed substrate, or a stuck-closed exhaust backpressure valve on vehicles so equipped.
safetyImpact: Turbo damage possible if ignored; severe power loss.

fixSteps.title: Check oil consumption
fixSteps.instruction: Confirm engine is not burning excessive oil.

fixSteps.title: DPF cleaning/replacement
fixSteps.instruction: Clean DPF or replace if contaminated.

faq.q: Can I just remove the DPF?
faq.a: No — illegal in the US and will cause multiple aftertreatment codes.

title: Closed Loop DPF Regeneration Control at Limit - Flow Too Low
shortDescription: DPF regeneration control detected flow below threshold.
fullDescription: P246D is set when the ECM's closed-loop control of DPF regen cannot achieve expected exhaust flow. This could be caused by a restricted DPF, a failed differential pressure sensor, or an air intake restriction preventing enough mass flow for full regen.
safetyImpact: Regen failures; progressive soot buildup.

fixSteps.title: Check air filter
fixSteps.instruction: Replace if clogged.

fixSteps.title: Check DPF load
fixSteps.instruction: Read soot load % via scan tool.

fixSteps.title: Force regen or clean DPF
fixSteps.instruction: Command stationary regen; clean if it fails.

faq.q: How long should a regen take?
faq.a: Typically 20-45 minutes of highway driving or 30-60 minutes stationary.

title: Exhaust Gas Recirculation Cooler Bypass Control Performance
shortDescription: EGR cooler bypass valve is not responding to ECM commands.
fullDescription:
P2490 sets when the EGR cooler bypass valve (used to warm up catalysts faster or to reduce EGR temperature) is mechanically stuck or the actuator has failed. This affects cold-start emissions and EGR temperature control.

Common on diesels where soot and condensation bind the bypass flap.
safetyImpact: Cold-start emissions; no immediate drivability issue.

fixSteps.title: Actuate valve
fixSteps.instruction: Use bidirectional scan tool to cycle bypass.

fixSteps.title: Clean or replace
fixSteps.instruction: Clean flap; replace actuator if unresponsive.

faq.q: Is this an emission-only code?
faq.a: Mostly — but some vehicles will eventually derate if unresolved.

title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve A Control Circuit
shortDescription: General circuit malfunction in the turbo bypass valve control.
fullDescription:
P0033 is set when the ECM detects an electrical fault on the turbo bypass (diverter/blow-off) valve control circuit. The bypass valve protects the turbo from compressor surge during throttle lift.

Electronic bypass valves are increasingly common; mechanical vacuum-actuated versions are not covered by this code.
safetyImpact: Possible turbo surge; minor drivability impact.

fixSteps.title: Inspect connector
fixSteps.instruction: Check plug for corrosion or damage.

fixSteps.title: Measure coil
fixSteps.instruction: Test solenoid resistance.

fixSteps.title: Replace valve
fixSteps.instruction: Replace bypass solenoid/valve.

faq.q: Will this hurt the turbo?
faq.a: Repeated compressor surge can damage the turbo over time.

title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve A Control Circuit Low
shortDescription: Low voltage condition on turbo bypass valve control circuit.
fullDescription: P0034 sets when the bypass valve control circuit voltage is below threshold — usually a short to ground or a shorted solenoid. The bypass valve may stay open, preventing boost from building properly.
safetyImpact: Loss of boost; sluggish acceleration.

causes.cause: Short to ground in control wire

fixSteps.title: Check wiring
fixSteps.instruction: Look for chafed control wire.

fixSteps.title: Replace solenoid
fixSteps.instruction: Replace bypass valve.

faq.q: Is a short the most common cause?
faq.a: Yes — heat-damaged insulation near the turbo is the usual culprit.

title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control A Circuit/Open
shortDescription: Open circuit detected in the turbo boost control A circuit.
fullDescription:
P0045 sets when the ECM cannot see a completed circuit to the boost control solenoid or VGT actuator. Common on diesels with VGT and gas turbos with electronic wastegates.

Inspect the connector and coil resistance; wiring damage from heat is common.
safetyImpact: Overboost or underboost; potential engine damage if overboost occurs.

fixSteps.title: Check connector
fixSteps.instruction: Ensure plug is fully seated.

fixSteps.title: Measure coil
fixSteps.instruction: Coil resistance should match spec.

fixSteps.title: Replace solenoid
fixSteps.instruction: Replace if coil is open.

faq.q: What happens to the turbo with this code?
faq.a: On most applications it defaults to minimum boost for safety.

title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control A Circuit Range/Performance
shortDescription: Boost control A circuit reading is out of expected range or not responding.
fullDescription: P0046 indicates the boost control actuator is not moving as expected in response to ECM commands. This is often mechanical (sticking VGT vanes on diesels) or electrical (solenoid losing precision). P0046 often accompanies P226F on VGT-equipped diesels.
safetyImpact: Boost error; derate.

fixSteps.title: Actuate VGT
fixSteps.instruction: Use scan tool to cycle VGT and compare commanded vs actual.

fixSteps.title: Clean or replace
fixSteps.instruction: Clean VGT or replace turbo/actuator as needed.

faq.q: Will cleaning fix this?
faq.a: Often on early-stage fouling; severe sticking needs turbo removal.

title: Turbocharger/Supercharger A Overboost Condition
shortDescription: Boost pressure exceeded the maximum allowed value.
fullDescription:
P0234 is set when measured boost exceeds the ECM's max threshold. Overboost is serious and can damage the engine, turbo, or intercooler.

Common causes include a stuck VGT vane, a failed wastegate, a disconnected boost control line, or an aftermarket boost controller incorrectly configured.
safetyImpact: Severe — can cause catastrophic engine damage. Reduce load immediately.

causes.cause: Failed boost sensor reporting wrong value

fixSteps.title: Reduce load immediately
fixSteps.instruction: Stop driving aggressively until diagnosed.

fixSteps.title: Check boost control lines
fixSteps.instruction: Inspect vacuum/boost lines for disconnections.

fixSteps.title: Test wastegate
fixSteps.instruction: Verify wastegate moves freely.

fixSteps.title: Repair/replace
fixSteps.instruction: Repair failed component.

faq.q: Can I drive to the shop?
faq.a: Yes if in limp mode and drive gently — but do not rev aggressively.

title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Sensor A Circuit
shortDescription: General electrical malfunction in the boost pressure sensor A circuit.
fullDescription: P0235 is set when the ECM detects an out-of-range or erratic signal on the boost (MAP or dedicated boost) pressure sensor circuit. Common causes are a failed sensor, damaged wiring near the intake, or a contaminated sensor port.
safetyImpact: Boost control may default to safe values, reducing power.

fixSteps.title: Inspect sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Check sensor for oil/soot contamination.

fixSteps.title: Check reference voltage
fixSteps.instruction: Confirm 5V reference at connector.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Replace boost sensor.

faq.q: Can soot cause this code?
faq.a: Yes — diesel intakes often accumulate oily soot that fouls boost sensors.

title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
shortDescription: Boost sensor A reading does not correlate with engine operating conditions.
fullDescription: P0236 indicates the boost sensor reading does not match expected values derived from engine load, RPM, and commanded boost. Typical causes: slow-responding sensor, boost leaks, or intake restrictions.
safetyImpact: Reduced power and boost control accuracy.

fixSteps.title: Smoke test intake
fixSteps.instruction: Locate boost leaks.

fixSteps.title: Replace filter
fixSteps.instruction: Replace air filter if restricted.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Replace boost sensor if out of spec.

faq.q: Can I drive with P0236?
faq.a: Usually yes in a reduced power state; repair soon to avoid other codes.

title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Sensor A Circuit High
shortDescription: Boost sensor A voltage is above the expected maximum.
fullDescription: P0238 sets when the boost sensor signal voltage exceeds the upper threshold, usually indicating a short to voltage, an open ground, or a failed sensor reporting maximum value.
safetyImpact: Limp mode likely due to uncertain boost feedback.

fixSteps.title: Check ground
fixSteps.instruction: Verify sensor ground.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Replace boost sensor.

faq.q: Does cleaning the sensor help?
faq.a: Sometimes — carbon buildup can skew readings high.

title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Sensor B Malfunction
shortDescription: Malfunction in the second boost pressure sensor circuit.
fullDescription: P0239 applies to engines with multiple boost sensors (e.g., twin-turbo or compound-turbo applications, or pre- and post-throttle sensors). It indicates the secondary sensor has failed or is out of range.
safetyImpact: Boost control precision reduced.

fixSteps.title: Inspect sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Check sensor and wiring.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Replace boost sensor B.

faq.q: Which engines have a B sensor?
faq.a: Typically twin-turbo, sequential turbo, or some bi-turbo diesels.

title: Turbocharger/Supercharger A Underboost Condition
shortDescription: Measured boost is below the minimum expected value.
fullDescription:
P0299 is one of the most common turbo codes. It indicates actual boost is lower than what the ECM commanded — often due to a boost leak, failed wastegate, sticking VGT, or failed turbo.

Start with a smoke test — boost leaks are the top cause.
safetyImpact: Reduced power; no immediate safety risk.

causes.cause: Clogged air filter or intake restriction

fixSteps.title: Smoke test intake
fixSteps.instruction: Locate and repair boost leaks.

fixSteps.title: Inspect wastegate
fixSteps.instruction: Verify wastegate function and actuator.

fixSteps.title: Clean VGT
fixSteps.instruction: Perform VGT clean or replace turbo.

faq.q: Could a loose clamp cause this?
faq.a: Absolutely — loose intercooler clamps are a top cause of P0299.

title: Turbocharger Wastegate Solenoid A Low
shortDescription: Wastegate solenoid A control circuit voltage is too low.
fullDescription: P0245 sets when the wastegate control solenoid circuit voltage falls below the ECM's expected range, suggesting a short to ground or a failed solenoid. The wastegate may default to a fail-safe position reducing boost.
safetyImpact: Reduced power until repaired.

fixSteps.title: Unplug solenoid
fixSteps.instruction: See if fault becomes open-circuit with connector off.

fixSteps.title: Test coil
fixSteps.instruction: Measure solenoid resistance.

fixSteps.title: Replace solenoid
fixSteps.instruction: Replace wastegate solenoid.

faq.q: Can I skip the solenoid test?
faq.a: Not recommended — it's the most common failure for this code family.

title: Turbocharger Wastegate Solenoid A High
shortDescription: Wastegate solenoid A control circuit voltage is too high.
fullDescription: P0246 is the counterpart to P0245 — the ECM sees excess voltage on the wastegate solenoid control line, usually from an open circuit or short to battery voltage.
safetyImpact: Reduced power; no immediate safety issue.

fixSteps.title: Check connector
fixSteps.instruction: Ensure connector is fully seated.

fixSteps.title: Test continuity
fixSteps.instruction: Verify control wire from ECM to solenoid.

fixSteps.title: Replace solenoid
fixSteps.instruction: Replace solenoid if open.

faq.q: Can heat damage the connector?
faq.a: Yes — turbo area connectors frequently degrade from heat cycling.

title: Turbocharger Wastegate Solenoid B Range/Performance
shortDescription: Wastegate solenoid B is not responding as expected to ECM commands.
fullDescription: P0247 sets on twin-turbo or dual-wastegate systems when solenoid B's behavior doesn't match expected performance. Could indicate a sticking solenoid, a leaking vacuum/boost line to the wastegate actuator, or a worn actuator.
safetyImpact: Boost imbalance between turbos; reduced power.

causes.cause: Cracked vacuum line to wastegate B

fixSteps.title: Inspect vacuum lines
fixSteps.instruction: Check all wastegate vacuum/boost lines for cracks.

fixSteps.title: Test actuator
fixSteps.instruction: Apply vacuum/pressure to actuator and check movement.

fixSteps.title: Replace as needed
fixSteps.instruction: Replace solenoid, line, or actuator.

faq.q: Which turbo is 'B'?
faq.a: Usually the secondary/sequential turbo — consult service info for your specific engine.

title: Turbocharger Wastegate Solenoid B Malfunction
shortDescription: General fault detected in wastegate solenoid B.
fullDescription: P0248 is the generic malfunction code for the B wastegate solenoid. Diagnose similar to P0245/P0246 — check wiring, coil resistance, and mechanical function.
safetyImpact: Boost control impaired.

fixSteps.title: Test solenoid
fixSteps.instruction: Check coil resistance.

fixSteps.title: Replace solenoid
fixSteps.instruction: Replace wastegate solenoid B.

faq.q: Is this the same as turbo B?
faq.a: Not exactly — refers to the wastegate solenoid labeled B, which on most engines controls turbo 2.

title: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor Circuit
shortDescription: General fault in the turbo VGT position feedback sensor circuit.
fullDescription: P2562 indicates a problem with the VGT position sensor circuit. The sensor provides feedback on the actual position of the turbo vanes or wastegate actuator. Without valid feedback, closed-loop boost control fails.
safetyImpact: Limp mode and derate are common.

fixSteps.title: Inspect wiring
fixSteps.instruction: Look for melted or chafed wiring near turbo.

fixSteps.title: Test sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Verify sensor signal with scan tool while actuating VGT.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor/actuator
fixSteps.instruction: Replace VGT position sensor or actuator assembly.

faq.q: Can I replace just the sensor?
faq.a: On some engines yes; others require the entire VGT actuator assembly.

title: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor Performance
shortDescription: VGT position sensor reading does not correlate with commanded position.
fullDescription:
P2563 sets when the VGT position sensor indicates the vanes are not moving as commanded. On diesels this is the classic 'stuck VGT' fault — soot has bound the vanes and they won't traverse their range.

VGT cleaning can often resolve it; advanced cases require turbo replacement.
safetyImpact: Derate and limp mode.

fixSteps.title: Clean VGT
fixSteps.instruction: Perform chemical VGT cleaning procedure.

fixSteps.title: Replace turbo/actuator
fixSteps.instruction: If cleaning fails, replace turbo.

faq.q: Does regen prevent VGT sticking?
faq.a: Yes — regular regens and highway driving minimize soot buildup.

title: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor Circuit Low
shortDescription: VGT position sensor signal voltage below minimum threshold.
fullDescription: P2564 indicates the VGT position sensor is reading a voltage below expected (typically under 0.3V). Causes include a short to ground, an open 5V reference, or a failed sensor.
safetyImpact: Derate.

causes.cause: Short to ground in signal wire

fixSteps.title: Check reference voltage
fixSteps.instruction: Probe 5V reference at sensor.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Replace VGT position sensor/actuator.

faq.q: Is heat the main enemy of this sensor?
faq.a: Yes — most failures are from cumulative heat exposure.

title: Knock Sensor 1 Circuit Malfunction (Bank 1 or Single Sensor)
shortDescription: General electrical fault in knock sensor 1 circuit.
fullDescription:
P0325 sets when the ECM detects a general electrical problem with knock sensor 1. The knock sensor allows ignition timing advance to optimal limits; without it, the ECM retards timing for safety.

Often caused by sensor failure, wire damage under the intake, or a corroded connector.
safetyImpact: Reduced power and MPG; minor risk of detonation under load.

fixSteps.title: Inspect wiring
fixSteps.instruction: Check harness routing over intake for damage.

fixSteps.title: Test sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Tap near sensor while observing knock activity on scan tool.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Replace knock sensor.

faq.q: Why is replacement labor-intensive?
faq.a: Knock sensors often sit under the intake manifold, requiring manifold removal.

title: Knock Sensor 1 Range/Performance (Bank 1 or Single Sensor)
shortDescription: Knock sensor 1 signal is out of expected range.
fullDescription: P0326 sets when the knock sensor signal amplitude or frequency is abnormal given engine operation. This often indicates an aging sensor or an engine mechanical issue generating unusual vibrations (loose accessory, bad flex plate).
safetyImpact: Timing retard; reduced power.

fixSteps.title: Check torque
fixSteps.instruction: Verify sensor mounting torque (usually 15-20 Nm).

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Replace knock sensor if out of spec.

faq.q: Can wrong torque cause this?
faq.a: Yes — knock sensors are torque-sensitive; over or under-tightened sensors misread.

title: Knock Sensor 1 Circuit Low Input (Bank 1 or Single Sensor)
shortDescription: Knock sensor 1 signal voltage is below threshold.
fullDescription: P0327 sets when the knock sensor signal voltage is lower than expected — typically a shorted-to-ground wire, failed sensor, or loose connection.
safetyImpact: Timing retard; reduced power.

fixSteps.title: Check wiring
fixSteps.instruction: Look for chafed wires to knock sensor.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Replace knock sensor.

faq.q: Is this repair a DIY job?
faq.a: Experienced DIYers can do it; intake removal is required on many engines.

title: Knock Sensor 1 Circuit High Input (Bank 1 or Single Sensor)
shortDescription: Knock sensor 1 signal voltage is above threshold.
fullDescription: P0328 sets when knock sensor 1's voltage is abnormally high — usually a short to voltage or a failed sensor.
safetyImpact: Timing retard; reduced power.

fixSteps.title: Check wiring
fixSteps.instruction: Inspect for shorts.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Replace knock sensor.

faq.q: Could a bad ground cause P0328?
faq.a: Yes — knock sensors are sensitive to ground integrity.

title: Knock Sensor 2 Circuit Malfunction (Bank 2)
shortDescription: General fault in the bank 2 knock sensor circuit.
fullDescription: P0330 is the bank 2 version of P0325 — applicable to V-engines with per-bank knock sensors. Diagnose identically, focused on bank 2 wiring and components.
safetyImpact: Timing retard on bank 2; reduced power.

fixSteps.title: Inspect bank 2 wiring
fixSteps.instruction: Trace harness to bank 2 knock sensor.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Replace bank 2 knock sensor.

faq.q: Is it best to replace both at once?
faq.a: Yes — labor overlap often makes replacing both sensors the economical choice.

title: Knock Sensor 2 Range/Performance (Bank 2)
shortDescription: Knock sensor 2 signal out of expected range.
fullDescription: P0331 indicates bank 2 knock sensor signal doesn't correlate with engine operation. Same diagnostic path as P0326 — verify mounting and replace if needed.
safetyImpact: Timing retard.

fixSteps.title: Verify mounting torque
fixSteps.instruction: Retighten to spec.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Replace if still out of spec.

faq.q: Can an internal engine noise trigger this?
faq.a: Yes — a worn bearing or accessory can generate vibrations that fool the sensor.

title: Knock Sensor 2 Circuit Low Input (Bank 2)
shortDescription: Knock sensor 2 signal voltage below threshold.
fullDescription: P0332 sets when the bank 2 knock sensor signal is too low, typically from a short to ground or a failed sensor coil.
safetyImpact: Reduced power on bank 2.

fixSteps.title: Check wiring
fixSteps.instruction: Inspect harness.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Replace bank 2 knock sensor.

faq.q: Could moisture cause this?
faq.a: Yes — water intrusion into the connector can short the signal.

title: Knock Sensor 2 Circuit High Input (Bank 2)
shortDescription: Knock sensor 2 signal voltage above threshold.
fullDescription: P0333 sets when the bank 2 knock sensor signal is too high — usually caused by a short to voltage or a failed sensor.
safetyImpact: Reduced power.

fixSteps.title: Check wiring
fixSteps.instruction: Check for shorts.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Replace bank 2 knock sensor.

faq.q: Will this hurt the engine?
faq.a: Not immediately — but prolonged operation with retarded timing reduces MPG.

title: Knock Sensor 2 Circuit Intermittent (Bank 2)
shortDescription: Bank 2 knock sensor signal is intermittently lost.
fullDescription: P0334 sets when the ECM sees periodic loss of signal from bank 2 knock sensor. This is commonly caused by a loose connector, a broken wire only seen under vibration, or a sensor about to fail.
safetyImpact: Intermittent power reduction.

fixSteps.title: Wiggle test
fixSteps.instruction: Wiggle harness while watching scan data for signal dropouts.

fixSteps.title: Reseat connector
fixSteps.instruction: Unplug and reseat; apply dielectric grease.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Replace sensor if faults return.

faq.q: Why does it come and go?
faq.a: Intermittent faults are often temperature- or vibration-dependent wiring issues.

title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve A Control Circuit High
shortDescription: Bypass valve A control circuit voltage above expected threshold.
fullDescription:
P0035 sets when the ECM detects abnormally high voltage on the turbo bypass valve control line, usually from an open circuit, disconnected solenoid, or short to battery voltage.

A disconnected bypass valve will allow compressor surge on throttle lift.
safetyImpact: Possible compressor surge.

fixSteps.title: Reseat connector
fixSteps.instruction: Verify bypass valve plug is seated.

fixSteps.title: Test wire
fixSteps.instruction: Check continuity from ECM.

fixSteps.title: Replace valve
fixSteps.instruction: Replace bypass valve.

faq.q: Does this protect the turbo?
faq.a: The bypass valve itself prevents surge — without it, the turbo is more stressed.

title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Sensor A Circuit Low
shortDescription: Boost sensor A voltage below expected minimum.
fullDescription: P0237 sets when the boost pressure sensor signal voltage is below threshold — typically a short to ground, contaminated sensor, or failed sensor stuck at minimum output.
safetyImpact: Reduced power; limp mode possible.

fixSteps.title: Clean sensor port
fixSteps.instruction: Remove soot/oil from intake port.

fixSteps.title: Check wiring
fixSteps.instruction: Test for shorts.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Replace boost sensor.

faq.q: Can a dirty intake trigger this?
faq.a: Yes — soot sealing the sensor port can cause low-voltage readings.

title: Knock Sensor 1 Circuit (Bank 1 or Single Sensor) - Primary
shortDescription: Primary knock sensor 1 circuit fault.
fullDescription:
P0325 indicates an electrical fault with the primary knock sensor circuit. The sensor allows the ECM to detect detonation and advance timing aggressively. When faulted, the ECM retards timing conservatively, reducing power and MPG.

Most common cause is a failed sensor — they age with heat exposure.
safetyImpact: Reduced power; MPG loss.

fixSteps.title: Read data
fixSteps.instruction: Check knock activity in live data.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Replace knock sensor.

faq.q: How long do knock sensors last?
faq.a: Typically 100k-150k miles before accuracy degrades.

title: Knock Sensor 1 Range/Performance - Primary
shortDescription: Primary knock sensor 1 out-of-range performance.
fullDescription: P0326 indicates the primary knock sensor signal doesn't match expected values for current engine load and RPM. A sensor that has drifted with age will often set this code before full failure.
safetyImpact: Reduced timing advance.

fixSteps.title: Verify fuel
fixSteps.instruction: Confirm correct octane fuel in tank.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Replace knock sensor.

faq.q: Does low-octane gas cause P0326?
faq.a: Indirectly — constant detonation input can skew sensor learning.

title: Intake Air Temperature Sensor 2 Circuit Range/Performance
shortDescription: IAT2 sensor reading is out of expected range.
fullDescription: P0096 sets when the secondary intake air temperature sensor reads outside the expected range compared to IAT1 or ambient sensor at key-on. On turbo engines this is typically the post-intercooler sensor.
safetyImpact: Minor boost/fuel trim error.

fixSteps.title: Compare sensors
fixSteps.instruction: Watch IAT1/IAT2 at cold start.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Replace IAT2.

faq.q: Is IAT2 always needed?
faq.a: On turbos yes — charge air temperature affects timing and boost maps.

title: Intake Air Temperature Sensor 2 Circuit Low
shortDescription: IAT2 signal voltage is below the expected minimum.
fullDescription: P0097 indicates the IAT2 signal voltage is too low, usually meaning a short to ground or a sensor reading maximum temperature (thermistors flip voltage inversely to temp).
safetyImpact: Fuel trim adjustment inaccuracy.

fixSteps.title: Check wiring
fixSteps.instruction: Look for pinched wire.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Replace IAT2.

faq.q: Will this cause hard start?
faq.a: Rarely — the ECM substitutes a default value when the sensor fails.

title: Intake Air Temperature Sensor 2 Circuit High
shortDescription: IAT2 signal voltage is above the expected maximum.
fullDescription: P0098 indicates the IAT2 signal voltage is too high, usually from an open circuit, disconnected sensor, or broken thermistor element.
safetyImpact: Minor fuel trim inaccuracy.

fixSteps.title: Check connector
fixSteps.instruction: Ensure sensor is plugged in.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Replace IAT2.

faq.q: Can cold weather trigger this?
faq.a: Not typically — the ECM expects a range that includes well below freezing.

title: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance Bank 1 Sensor 2
shortDescription: EGT sensor 2 on bank 1 is outside expected range or response spec.
fullDescription:
P2084 indicates the second EGT sensor on bank 1 (typically post-DPF or post-DOC) is reporting values inconsistent with expected temperature gradients. On diesels this is critical for regeneration temperature control and aftertreatment protection.

Check for soot around the sensor tip, heat-damaged wiring, or drift that shows up at steady state.
safetyImpact: Regen may be blocked; emissions non-compliance.

fixSteps.title: Compare EGT sensors
fixSteps.instruction: Look at EGT1/EGT2/EGT3 alignment at steady load.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Replace EGT sensor 2 if drifted.

faq.q: How often do EGT sensors fail?
faq.a: Around 100-150k miles is typical on hard-working diesels.
